chapterName: Middle Republic: Scipio and the Road to Zama (216-201 BCE)

briefing.title: Cannae, 216 BC
paragraphs: It is 216 BC, and Rome is reeling. Hannibal, the general of Carthage, a great trading city on the coast of modern Tunisia, has marched an army from Spain over the Alps. At Cannae in southern Italy he has crushed the Romans: at least 67,500 lie dead or captured.

Among the survivors is a young officer named Scipio. Within a few years Rome will hand him an army, though he has held no senior office. Can he win back Spain, carry the war to Africa and face Hannibal himself?

timelines.name: Level 1: The Big Turning Points
timelines.blurb: Four milestones from disaster to final victory.

events.label: Disaster at Cannae
events.fact: At least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured at Cannae, but the young Scipio survived and rallied the stragglers.

events.label: Scipio storms New Carthage
events.fact: Scipio sent a party across the lagoon at low tide and captured Carthage's main supply base in Spain.

events.label: Battle of Zama
events.fact: Scipio defeated Hannibal near Zama, in what is now Tunisia, after the Roman cavalry struck the Carthaginian rear.

events.label: Rome destroys Carthage
events.fact: Long after the harsh peace of 201 BC had made Carthage subordinate, Rome destroyed the city altogether.

timelines.name: Level 2: From the Alps to the Peace
timelines.blurb: Follow the war from Hannibal's invasion to Carthage's surrender.

events.label: Hannibal crosses the Alps into Italy
events.fact: Hannibal's march from Spain over the Alps started the Second Punic War.

events.label: Scipio elected aedile
events.fact: A tribune objected that Scipio was too young to be aedile, the official for streets and festivals, but the crowd's enthusiasm made him back down.

events.label: Scipio's father and uncle killed in Spain
events.fact: The brothers split their forces to attack three enemy armies at once and were each beaten separately.

events.label: Battle of the Metaurus
events.fact: Claudius Nero's flank attack destroyed the army of Hannibal's brother beside the Metaurus river in north-east Italy.

events.label: Scipio lands in Africa near Utica
events.fact: Scipio's fleet landed about 20 km (12 miles) north of Utica, a major Carthaginian port, and Masinissa joined him.

events.label: Carthage accepts Rome's peace terms
events.fact: Carthage had to pay 10,000 silver talents over 50 years and keep only ten warships.

timelines.name: Level 3: Scipio's Rise Step by Step
timelines.blurb: Eight moments in the career of Scipio and the story of how we know it.

events.label: Cavalry clash on the river Ticinus
events.fact: One ancient account says young Scipio saved his surrounded father here; other writers credited an unnamed slave.

events.label: Scipio given the Spanish command
events.fact: At about 25, Scipio became the first Roman given a consul's military authority without first serving as consul.

events.label: Battle of Baecula
events.fact: Scipio won the battle, but Hannibal's brother slipped away with most of his army and headed for Italy.

events.label: Decisive victory at Ilipa
events.fact: At Ilipa, north of modern Seville, Scipio routed the remaining Carthaginian forces and drove them from Spain.

events.label: Scipio serves as consul at 31
events.fact: The normal minimum age for consul was 42, yet Scipio was elected amid wild enthusiasm.

events.label: Enemy camps burned at night
events.fact: Scipio set the Numidian camp's reed huts ablaze and then fell on the Carthaginian camp, killing thousands in the dark.

events.label: Scipio's triumph as Africanus
events.fact: Scipio paraded through Rome, took the surname Africanus and deposited about 40 tonnes (123,000 Roman pounds) of silver in the treasury.

events.label: Polybius sent to Rome as a hostage
events.fact: Polybius, the Greek historian who is our main surviving source on Scipio, came to Rome as a hostage.

matchSets.name: People and Names
matchSets.blurb: Match each name to the role it played in the war.

pairs.name: Hannibal
pairs.match: Carthaginian general who marched from Spain over the Alps into Italy

pairs.name: Claudius Nero
pairs.match: Consul who marched north in secret to win at the Metaurus

pairs.name: Masinissa
pairs.match: Numidian prince who left Carthage to become Rome's best ally

pairs.name: Polybius
pairs.match: Greek historian, once a hostage in Rome; our most reliable source

pairs.name: Africanus
pairs.match: Honorary surname Scipio took after his victory over Carthage

matchSets.name: Roman Offices and Terms
matchSets.blurb: Match each Roman term to its meaning.

pairs.name: Consul
pairs.match: One of two magistrates elected each year to lead Rome's armies

pairs.name: Aedile
pairs.match: Official who looked after the city's streets and festivals

pairs.name: Military tribune
pairs.match: Junior officer; the rank Scipio held at Cannae

pairs.name: Velites
pairs.match: Light skirmishers who filled the open lanes at Zama

pairs.name: Princeps senatus
pairs.match: Leader of the Senate, who fought Scipio's plan to invade Africa

trueFalseDecks.name: Italy and Spain
trueFalseDecks.blurb: From Cannae to the conquest of Spain and the Metaurus.

cards.claim: At Cannae at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.
cards.why: The chapter gives at least 67,500 Romans killed or captured at Cannae, including Scipio's future father-in-law, a consul.

cards.claim: Scipio had already served as consul before he received the Spanish command.
cards.why: Scipio had held none of Rome's senior offices. He was the first Roman given a consul's military authority without first serving as consul.

cards.claim: The lagoon guarding New Carthage's northern side could be waded at low tide.
cards.why: Scipio sent a party across the lagoon at low tide while the walls were under attack.

cards.claim: At New Carthage Scipio told his troops that the war god Mars had promised him help in a vision.
cards.why: Scipio claimed the sea god Neptune had promised him help, feeding the legend that he was a favourite of the gods.

cards.claim: At Baecula Scipio destroyed the whole army of Hannibal's brother.
cards.why: Scipio won the battle, but his opponent slipped away with most of his army, crossed the Pyrenees and headed for Italy.

cards.claim: Italica, a town Scipio founded near Seville, later became the birthplace of three Roman emperors.
cards.why: Scipio founded Italica about 9 km northwest of Seville, and three Roman emperors were later born there.

cards.claim: Claudius Nero marched north with 7,000 picked men without waiting for the Senate's approval.
cards.why: After reading the captured letters, Claudius Nero marched north in secret, gathering volunteers and supplies on the way.

cards.claim: After the Metaurus, Hannibal marched straight on Rome.
cards.why: After his brother's head was thrown into his camp, Hannibal withdrew to Bruttium, the 'toe' of Italy.

trueFalseDecks.name: Africa, Zama and the Sources
trueFalseDecks.blurb: From the debate in the Senate to the peace and the legend.

cards.claim: Scipio was elected consul at 31, although the normal minimum age was 42.
cards.why: He was elected consul for 205 BC amid wild enthusiasm at 31, well below the usual minimum age of 42.

cards.claim: The core of Scipio's army in Sicily was two legions of Cannae survivors.
cards.why: Scipio could only ask for volunteers, and his core force was two legions of Cannae survivors posted to Sicily.

cards.claim: In 204 BC Scipio's fleet landed about 20 km (12 miles) north of Carthage itself.
cards.why: The fleet landed about 20 km (12 miles) north of Utica, a major Carthaginian port, which Scipio then besieged.

cards.claim: During winter peace talks, Scipio's envoys secretly studied the enemy camps and their reed huts.
cards.why: The envoys used each visit to study the camps' layout, exits and huts of reeds, which Scipio later set ablaze.

cards.claim: At Zama Hannibal had more cavalry than Scipio.
cards.why: Hannibal had only 4,000 cavalry, while Scipio had more than 6,000, many of them brought by Masinissa.

cards.claim: Under the peace of 201 BC Carthage had to pay 10,000 silver talents over 50 years.
cards.why: Carthage also gave up its war elephants, kept only ten warships and could not wage war outside Africa.

cards.claim: After Zama Scipio accepted his admirers' offer to make him dictator for life.
cards.why: Scipio refused to become consul for life and dictator, a restraint later Roman writers praised.

cards.claim: Scipio's own memoirs, written in Greek, survive and are our main source about him.
cards.why: His memoirs are lost. What survives comes mainly from Polybius, the Greek historian.

oddOneOut.why: Baecula, Ilipa and Gades are in southern Spain, which Scipio won from Carthage; Utica is a Carthaginian port in Africa that he besieged in 204 BC.
Scipio won at Baecula, Ilipa and New Carthage, all in Spain; the Metaurus was won in Italy by Claudius Nero and his fellow consul.
Scipio served as military tribune, aedile and consul. When admirers urged him to become dictator, he refused.
The first three were terms of the peace of 201 BC. Carthage did not lose every warship: it kept ten.
Three happened in the battle of Zama in 202 BC. The burning of the reed-hut camps was Scipio's night attack in 203 BC.

items: Scipio as a son of Jupiter
oddOneOut.why: The oath story, Hannibal's ranking of generals and Scipio's divine birth are legends historians doubt. Claudius Nero's march north is told as solid history.
Three describe New Carthage, stormed in 209 BC. Carthage's last stronghold in Spain was Gades, modern Cádiz.

whoAmI.name: Commanders at War
whoAmI.blurb: Generals who fought in Italy and Spain.

people.name: Scipio
clues: Voters made me aedile in 213 BC, though a tribune said I was too young.
I served as a military tribune at Cannae and rallied the stragglers.
At about 25 I received a consul's authority without ever having been consul.
I stormed New Carthage after telling my troops that Neptune had promised me help.

people.name: Claudius Nero
clues: I had a dead enemy commander's head thrown into his brother's camp.
In 207 BC I was the consul shadowing Hannibal in the far south of Italy.
Without waiting for the Senate's approval, I marched 7,000 picked men north in secret.
My flank attack won the battle beside the Metaurus river.

people.name: Hannibal
clues: Recalled from Italy, I landed in Africa with 15,000 to 20,000 veterans.
After my defeat I told Carthage's leaders to make peace on whatever terms they could get.
Two of my brothers helped beat and kill Scipio's father and uncle in Spain.
In 218 BC I marched an army from Spain over the Alps into Italy.

whoAmI.name: Africa and After
whoAmI.blurb: An ally, a victor and the historian who told their story.

people.name: Masinissa
clues: As a young Numidian prince I fought for Carthage in Spain.
When a rival drove me from my kingdom, I joined Rome.
I helped hunt down the rival Numidian king and took over much of his kingdom.
Many of the horsemen who gave Rome its cavalry edge at Zama were mine.

people.name: Scipio
clues: In Sicily I drilled an army built around Cannae survivors for about a year.
My envoys studied enemy camps of reed huts, which I later set ablaze.
Admirers urged me to become consul for life and dictator, but I refused.
After beating Hannibal at Zama, I took the surname Africanus.

people.name: Polybius
clues: My main informant about Scipio was his friend and second-in-command.
I counted 20,000 Carthaginians killed at Zama against 1,500 Roman dead.
I argued that Scipio won through careful planning, not the favour of the gods.
Born a Greek around 200 BC, I was sent to Rome as a hostage in 167 BC.

places.name: Cannae
places.why: In southern Italy, where at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured in 216 BC and the young Scipio survived as a military tribune.

places.name: New Carthage
places.why: Carthage's main supply base in Spain, stormed by Scipio in 209 BC across a lagoon waded at low tide.

places.name: Ilipa
places.why: North of modern Seville, where Scipio's decisive victory in 206 BC drove the Carthaginians from Spain.

places.name: Metaurus
places.why: River in north-east Italy where Claudius Nero's flank attack destroyed the army of Hannibal's brother in 207 BC.

places.name: Sicily
places.why: Scipio's province in 205 BC, where he drilled his army of volunteers and Cannae survivors before crossing to Africa.

places.name: Utica
places.why: Major Carthaginian port that Scipio besieged after landing in Africa in 204 BC; it held out.

places.name: Zama
places.why: In what is now Tunisia, where Scipio defeated Hannibal in 202 BC and ended the war.
